## Observation

On 2026-10-28 the on-box MCP container (`rebar-mcp-e2ed08b343a2-8092`, limit 3,892,314,112 bytes) went from 0.93 GB resident (`rebar-health` sample 15:29:23 PDT) to 3.28 GB (15:34:23 PDT) and stayed between 3.16 and 3.41 GB for 2 hours 12 minutes, until the kernel OOM-killed it at 17:47:26 PDT when a batch of concurrent reads arrived (bug teenage-unquieted-ringworm).

The container log with timestamps (`docker logs -t`) shows tool calls (`CallToolRequest`) between 15:22 and 15:29:40 PDT, including plan-review gate activity (an admission warning for pyrite-cockeyed-gannet at 15:26:52). From 15:29:40 to 15:38 it shows only `PingRequest`. So the 2.3 GB rise happened with no request in flight.

For comparison, measured in the MCP image on Linux: 9 concurrent `next_batch` calls return their memory afterwards (peak 4,966 MB, 201 MB after), and a second burst peaks no higher than the first. Store-wide reads do not explain a plateau that lasts hours.

## Not established

What held the memory. Candidates to test: a background gate job (`review_plan_start` / `verify_completion_start` run on a daemon thread and outlive the request), a detached post-close compaction worker, or another child process inside the container. `rebar-health` samples container-wide RSS, so a child process counts.

## Acceptance Criteria

- [ ] The process or thread holding the memory during a plateau is identified with evidence (for example `docker top` plus per-process RSS, or a per-job memory log) and recorded here.
- [ ] Either the holder releases its memory when its work ends, or its memory is bounded and documented against the container limit.
- [ ] A test or probe that would fail if a finished background job keeps its memory.
compiled_state.title: MCP container holds about 2.3 GB for hours after background work with no request in flight
